title_en: The 5 Best Gaming Earbuds: Our Top Tested & Reviewed Picks for 2026
summary_en: Start gaming without a bulky headset and get yourself a pair of earbuds that sound just as good.
body_en:
After spending weeks testing 13 of the best earbuds for gaming, the SteelSeries Arctis GameBuds stand out because of their comfortable fit, balanced audio, and massive library of built-in equalizers that adapt your sound to specific games.
But players who need an open-ear design or strong noise canceling for their commute should pick a different set of gaming earbuds. Here's why.
I'm a journalist and reviewer with more than 12 years of experience writing about games and tech. I reviewed my first audio product seven years ago, and for the past year I've been IGN's lead earbud reviewer, primarily testing gaming earbuds that pack a wireless USB dongle for their connection to your PC or console, rather than relying on higher-latency Bluetooth.
Great gaming earbuds must tick lots of boxes: they should be comfortable to wear for long stretches, hold enough charge for long gaming sessions, and deliver audio without any significant delays. They should sound clean, balanced, and rich when playing games in any genre, and should clearly distinguish between audio elements. Ideally they'll tell you the directions of in-game sounds, such as an enemy's footsteps. They should, in most cases, have a decent microphone. And they must connect quickly and reliably across multiple gaming devices.
I consider some other features useful but not essential for gaming, including powerful noise canceling and a transparency mode.
I prioritized dedicated "gaming" earbuds. These buds usually include a USB-C dongle that you can plug into your PC, PS5, Switch or Steam Deck, reducing the latency of your connection. Bluetooth is fine for some casual games, especially with high-end modern earbuds, but if you pay attention you can notice a delay between the action and your audio – not ideal. Still, a couple of non-gaming earbuds made my longlist by virtue of their repeated recommendations elsewhere.
I made sure I selected earbuds that would work with PC and a variety of consoles, including some for Xbox (because of Xbox's proprietary wireless tech, only certain earbuds work with Microsoft’s console). I also wanted to accommodate a variety of price ranges, so I made sure to include multiple budget options that cost $50 or less.
After all of this, my longlist stretched to 25 earbuds. The next step was to whittle down to a shortlist of around a dozen for hands-on testing.
I researched every earbud on my longlist in detail, seeking out more reviews by critics and users. Any that appeared to have consistent quality-control issues or nagging flaws, I eliminated. I also eliminated any that were not widely available or appeared to be discontinued (for example, Logitech's G333 earbuds are often recommended, but aren't in stock in official stores).
I decided that I would cut any earbuds that did not have a dedicated lower-latency mode. This is a guide for buying earbuds specifically for gaming , so I wanted to recommend buds that will work across the board, not just for casual gaming. That meant earbuds like my beloved Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 4 Earbuds – which can achieve low latency, but only with an extra dongle purchased separately – were gone, as were the brilliant-sounding Technics EAH-AZ100 earbuds, whose lower-latency mode only works on phones.
I also started to consider my subcategories at this stage. I decided I wanted a budget pick, an open–ear pick, and a pick for earbuds that worked for everyday use alongside gaming. Thinking of my longlist in this context helped me whittle it down: I could, for example, cut out the HyperX Cloud Mix Buds 2: having reviewed them, I knew they didn't have a chance to win any of my categories.
After finalizing my shortlist, I called in products from manufacturers and began testing.
It’s worth noting, there were a few earbuds on my shortlist that I wasn’t able to get my hands on in time for this round of testing, namely Logitech's G Fits, the Sony WF-1000XM6 and the Truthear Hexa. I will endeavor to test them soon and when I do, I'll update this guide.
I tested each pair of earbuds, although I often swapped between buds to compare them. Not every earbud made it through to the end of my testing: If it was clear after a couple of hours that I would not recommend them, I moved on.
I started by simply opening the case, assessing its quality, and then feeling the buds in my hand. I squeezed them and swivelled them – I wanted to know how sturdy they were, how cheap or premium they felt. I then popped the buds in my ears without any sound, feeling the fit and deciding whether I needed to adjust the size of the eartips (most came with various sizes).
Given that I was testing buds for gaming, that's where I spent most of my time. I put the buds in their lowest-latency mode, either through the dongle or a dedicated Bluetooth gaming mode, and jumped straight into a couple of games on my PC. My go-tos were Marathon and GTA 5. These, I felt, tested the full range of audio capabilities.
Marathon's complex sound design – gunshots, footsteps, abilities, item noises, and background audio all at once – tested the earbuds' detail and clarity. I was looking for distinctions between each noise, plus a sense of distance and directionality, which are vital in a multiplayer shooter like this. It was also easy to notice any delays between gunshots and their audio (although I performed a standalone latency test outside of the game later on).
GTA 5, meanwhile, tested the buds' auditory punch, and how well they created a sense of atmosphere. I moved between roaming the city, driving with radio stations, dialogue, and gunfights.
At this stage I had been wearing the buds for a couple of hours, so I could tell how comfortable they were and also how their battery compared to the manufacturers' promise (I consider five hours to be fine for earbuds, and 10+ hours to be elite).
Then I conducted one simple latency test, and one for noise canceling.
For latency, I used an online tool called Sound Tester . The tool performs a "control" test of your reaction time by asking you to click when a light flashes – then, you close your eyes and click whenever you hear a beep. I wouldn't trust that the figures are fully accurate to the millisecond but I got a ballpark figure for latency and, crucially, could compare latency between buds. I conducted the test five times per set of earbuds and took an average.
For noise canceling, I turned the setting to maximum and wore the buds around the house, seeing how well they cut out the sound of a person speaking, the whirr of a fridge, the TV, and background music. For a slightly more objective test, I played some white noise through the buds at a set level each time and some pink noise through a speaker. I stood the same distance away from the speaker each time and turned up the volume of the pink noise until it was clearly distinguishable. The higher the volume, the better the noise canceling.
Away from PC, I tried the buds on the Nintendo Switch 2, PS5 (via a USB dongle) and Steam Deck: for the games I picked The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild on Switch, Astro Bot on PS5, and the plinky-plonk sounds of Balatro on Steam Deck. I was testing the audio quality in each case, but also the connection. Were they easy to connect to the console? Was the connection stable and reliable throughout my playing? Were there noticeable differences between each console?
After this stage the bulk of my testing was done, but for those buds still in contention of being a top pick, I used them in more mundane scenarios. A walk in the park, a bus ride, a gym session. I also listened to podcasts and to music, making sure I heard, at a minimum, the same two tracks with each buds: Dave's bassy rap track "100M's," and the complex orchestral Britpop of "Bitter Sweet Symphony" by The Verve. I also used them in a bunch of other games across my various consoles, including EA FC 26, Dishonored 2, Slay the Spire 2, and Super Mario Odyssey.
Throughout my testing I used the dedicated app for each bud, where it was available, assessing its depth and ease of use. I was also tapping the buds constantly to test their touch controls.
I had extensively tested some of the shortlisted earbuds already for existing reviews. In those cases I re-tested them to see if my initial verdict stood.
They sound rich and clear in every genre . The SteelSeries Arctis Gamebuds are a balanced, lively pair of earbuds that sound consistently good. Gunshots punch and echo, rain pitter patters, music thrums. No one element dominates and I always felt I could pick out individual details of a game's soundscape. Outside of games they're not as rich as the absolute best earbuds, but I enjoyed the vocal clarity of podcasts and listening to music: while they're not particularly bassy, I still felt a thump.
You can customize them easily to fit the game you're playing. The GameBuds app is relatively sparse, but its library of equalizers – EQs – is massive. EQs boost or dampen parts of the audio frequency range to create a different sound profile, and the GameBuds have prebuilt EQs for hundreds of individual games. I loved how easy it was to boot up a game, open the app, and tap a few buttons to get sound tailored to what I was about to play. The EQs meaningfully changed the audio and, in nearly every case, made it sound better. I also enjoyed selecting EQs from different games until I found one that suited my ears.
It's obvious where sounds are coming from. This helps create atmosphere in games such as Breath of the Wild when a fire crackles behind you, but it's arguably most important in multiplayer shooters. Guessing an enemy's direction and rough distance from their footsteps, gunshots and gadgets creates a huge advantage – the GameBuds won't be as good as over-ear headphones at this, but I still felt confident that I knew exactly what was going on around me. I could, for example, pinpoint the exact location of a buzzing claymore in Marathon.
They can last up to 10 hours on a single charge. That's the official figure: in practice, I got between eight and nine hours, but I was also draining the battery by flicking between noise canceling and transparency mode, constantly adjusting EQs, and swapping devices. I felt confident these buds would last through even my longest gaming sessions, and with three full charges in the case you can probably go a week between plugging them in.
They connect quickly and switch between devices seamlessly. I had zero issues switching between PC and consoles, whether I was using the USB dongle or Bluetooth. They always connected fast, and never dropped signal. Notably, they can simultaneously connect to your console through the USB dongle and to your phone via Bluetooth. Not every bud can manage this, and it meant I could fiddle with the EQs on my phone app while playing.
They'll work on every console, including Xbox. You'll need to buy a specific Xbox version of the earbuds if you want to play on Microsoft's console, but it will also work on PS5, PC, Switch and Steam Deck (it comes with a small switch in the dongle to flip between Xbox and everything else).
Their physical button is more reliable than touch controls. This is personal preference, but I find physical buttons far more reliable than tapping, hoping that your input has registered. The GameBuds' button is snappy and reliable.
They're comfortable to wear all day. Everyone's ears are different, but they fit me well. They never irritated my ears and when I wore them for a walk or run I felt no discomfort. Most other reviewers agree.
Their ANC and mic are good enough. The ANC was below-average among the buds I tested, and the mic is merely passable. I still think they're fine for most people: they'll reduce surrounding noise so you can focus on the game, and your teammates will still be able to hear your call-outs.
The best sounding gaming earbuds I've ever used. The Sony InZone Buds are rich, bassy, and clear. I loved the atmosphere they created in Breath of the Wild, the music interplaying with the whoosh of the wind. They use the same drivers as some of Sony's high-end audiophile earbuds, and it shows: I'd happily wear them everyday and listen to my favourite tracks. They're mega expensive at $240, but you get the sound you pay for.
Every footstep is clear and obvious. In Marathon, these buds gave me so much information: I could hear both the direction of other runners and their distance from me. I could distinguish between multiple sets of footsteps, and I could clearly tell the difference between healing items, even at a distance. The "Spatial Sound" setting in the Inzone app amplified everything.
Sony's PC-only app is comprehensive. On top of Spatial Sound, you can switch between thoughtful equalizer options, including one dedicated to footsteps and gunshots, and tweak the dynamic range to boost quieter sounds. Other bells and whistles include sound field personalization and sound tone personalization, which conduct a series of hearing tests and then tunes your audio. It's a generous tool set.
They last more than 11 hours on a single charge. Session-for-session, they're the longest-lasting dedicated gaming buds and even if you played all day, you'd still have some juice left. They lack both fast and wireless charging, and the case itself holds fewer charges than other buds, but the single-charge lifespan makes up for it.
Their looser fit is comfortable. Some earbuds really stick into you but the Inzone buds are slightly looser in my ear canals. That sacrifices a smidgeon of noise canceling – still fine – and means they don't quite match the sound of Sony's high-end non-gaming earbuds, despite having the same drivers. But the advantage is that you can wear them forever without aching.
They look distinctive. Style is subjective, of course, but you can't deny that they're so very Sony . The colors, the sharp angles, the smooth, reflective surface of the touch area. They look like a gaming accessory, and the bold design stands out on my desk.
Their connection is reliable and stable – but doesn't work with everything. I never dropped a connection when I was playing, but they won't link up with every device. They only support Bluetooth LE, which limits them to modern Android phones for Bluetooth, so you'll have to plug the dongle in every time you play on your PC, Switch, Steam Deck, or PS5 (they, like many other earbuds, don't work with Xbox). Unfortunately, the dongle sticks out more than others and feels wobbly. It's not fatal to these buds, but it's annoying.
They are stylish and solid. Sub-$50 earbuds never feel this good, and they use their higher-quality materials in all the right places. Both the cable and the buds are light, but they're finished with a metallic material that is reassuringly sturdy. The design feels like it blends modern and retro aesthetics into something elegant.
They sound brilliant for the money. I liked their sound profile more than some buds that were far more expensive. Clean and smooth are the two words that come to mind: They're bassy enough for most people but it's in the mid-ranges and the splash of high notes that they come alive. They sound natural, no one element dominates, and their soundscape feels wide and detailed. I especially loved listening to the playful melodies of Astro Bot, punctuated by the ping of collecting coins.
They're surprisingly comfortable. I worried about the foam eartips, but I needn't. Their flat shape stayed fixed in my ear, never sliding around or rubbing against my skin. Some people are irritated by eartips sticking into their ear canal – this design avoids that problem.
The high-quality cable never tangles. The braided cable is fully flexible but holds its shape just enough that it won't curl up into a ball: I never had to untangle it when I opened up the handy carry case to play a game. It's also fully detachable from the buds, if ever you need to repair it or swap it out for something longer.
They'll work with Xbox. I tested the 3.5mm headphone jack version of these buds, which doesn't work with my phone but does with everything else, including modern Xbox consoles. Having a wire can feel unwieldy if you're used to wireless buds, but I like the flexibility of being able to connect instantly to anything with an audio socket – such as an Xbox or PS5 controller – with zero setup.
You can choose a USB-C version if you want a mic. The model I tested has no mic, so when I played multiplayer I had to use a separate one I already own. If you don't have a mic and need one with your headphones, they Sivga sells a USB-C version with a mic. This model supports Hi-Res audio and so should sound slightly better, in ideal conditions. Just keep in mind that you won't be able to connect to your PS5 or Xbox consoles with it, although Switch, PC and Steam Deck will work fine.
You're sacrificing nonessential features. For this price you're always compromising but I don't think the lack of features damages its gaming credentials. You don't get noise canceling, but most people play games inside in a room that's at least relatively quiet. You need to put up with a wire, but again, when you're playing a game you're normally sat in one comfortable position rather than moving around, so you can easily forget the wire exists. And while the audio isn't top-tier, it's still fantastic.
They keep you aware of your surroundings. The Asus Rog Cetra Open are the only dedicated gaming buds I've seen with an open-ear design. While most gaming earbuds use a "transparency mode" to amplify external noise, these earbuds simply sit on your ears, rather than in them, leaving space for sounds to pass through. I could play while still hearing a delivery at the doorbell, or my newborn waking up from a nap.
They're the most comfortable gaming earbuds. The bonus of the design is that your inner ear never touches the buds, so there's no chance of discomfort. The straps that go around your ear, and the cylinder that holds them in place, are chunky and ugly but they never budge or chafe. I could happily wear them all day, and overnight too. I've also been running with these buds without any problems.
Their sound isn't the most detailed, but it's still immersive. Their audio weaknesses match those of other open-ear buds: they feel less immediate and less detailed, because there's simply more space before the sound source and your inner ear (think of the difference between somebody talking next to you versus across the room). They're not my favorite for music but in games like Breath of the Wild they still create a wide, immersive soundscape with plenty of depth. And in Marathon, I could still pinpoint enemy footsteps and gunshots.
They last a long time. Asus says you can get up to 16 hours straight with them, but that's with no Bluetooth, a muted mic, and no RGB lighting. For me, they've lasted between 8 and 10 hours, depending on my settings – that still makes them one of the longest-lasting gaming earbuds.
They're one of the few earbuds with pass-through charging on their USB dongle. The Steam Deck and the Switch have a single USB port on the top, so plugging in an earbud dongle blocks charging. Asus' dongle, however, has its own USB-C port on it, and you can plug your charger into that, charging the console at the same time as you're using the buds. It's a cool – and genuinely useful – party trick
But they're not perfect. As well as their chunky price, you have to deal with a massive, clunky case and a slightly confusing companion app. Remember too that their design makes noise canceling virtually impossible. They therefore aren't for everyone – but for some people, these are the best pick.
They're wonderfully built. The metal case is hefty and feels more solid than anything else I tested, and a rubber portion on the bottom stops it from scratching your desk. The buds themselves are compact and attractive – I like the contrast between the transparent section that reveals their innards and their plain black body. They, too, feel premium, and the Jlab logo lends texture to the touch area.
They're comfortable for runs or the commute. I used these buds at the gym, where they stayed securely in my ears, and enjoyed listening to podcasts during a two-hour walk. They canceled more noise than most of the buds I tested, making them viable buds for everyday use – they don't match the absolute best noise-canceling buds like the Bose QuietComfort Ultra but they're good enough for working in a busy cafe or traveling on a bus.
They sound bassy and powerful. When I first used them, music sounded slightly muddy. But fiddling with the EQs – there are three presets, plus a fully-customizable option – quickly landed me somewhere I liked, with powerful bass that didn't overwhelm vocals or instruments. In Dave's "100M's" these buds clearly separate the vocals, bass, synthesiser and the crisp hi-hats. I like how they sounded while gaming, and their detail shines in atmospheric games like Breath of the Wild.
The low-latency dongle matches dedicated gaming buds. These aren't made for gaming, but the USB-C dongle cuts the latency as well as the best gaming buds I tested. On PC, Steam Deck and Switch, my connection felt instant and responsive. They work with PS5 too, but weirdly their volume is limited to 20%. I could boost the volume through the console's Audio Focus settings, reaching a level that was playable in a quiet room, but it's not ideal and I hope Jlab fixed it.
They last a long time. JLab says they'll last up to 13 hours. If you're gaming with the dongle and tweaking settings in the app, you're not going to reach anywhere near that, but you should still get 8 hours from them. Then, when you're out and about, flip to Bluetooth to save your juice. The case holds more than three full charges, too.

They use the same drivers as some of Sony's high-end audiophile earbuds, and it shows: I'd happily wear them everyday and listen to my favourite tracks. They're mega expensive at $240, but you get the sound you pay for.

Every footstep is clear and obvious. In Marathon, these buds gave me so much information: I could hear both the direction of other runners and their distance from me. I could distinguish between multiple sets of footsteps, and I could clearly tell the difference between healing items, even at a distance. The "Spatial Sound" setting in the Inzone app amplified everything.

Sony's PC-only app is comprehensive. On top of Spatial Sound, you can switch between thoughtful equalizer options, including one dedicated to footsteps and gunshots, and tweak the dynamic range to boost quieter sounds. Other bells and whistles include sound field personalization and sound tone personalization, which conduct a series of hearing tests and then tunes your audio. It's a generous tool set.

They last more than 11 hours on a single charge. Session-for-session, they're the longest-lasting dedicated gaming buds and even if you played all day, you'd still have some juice left. They lack both fast and wireless charging, and the case itself holds fewer charges than other buds, but the single-charge lifespan makes up for it.

Their looser fit is comfortable. Some earbuds really stick into you but the Inzone buds are slightly looser in my ear canals. That sacrifices a smidgeon of noise canceling – still fine – and means they don't quite match the sound of Sony's high-end non-gaming earbuds, despite having the same drivers. But the advantage is that you can wear them forever without aching.

They look distinctive. Style is subjective, of course, but you can't deny that they're so very Sony . The colors, the sharp angles, the smooth, reflective surface of the touch area. They look like a gaming accessory, and the bold design stands out on my desk.

Their connection is reliable and stable – but doesn't work with everything. I never dropped a connection when I was playing, but they won't link up with every device. They only support Bluetooth LE, which limits them to modern Android phones for Bluetooth, so you'll have to plug the dongle in every time you play on your PC, Switch, Steam Deck, or PS5 (they, like many other earbuds, don't work with Xbox). Unfortunately, the dongle sticks out more than others and feels wobbly. It's not fatal to these buds, but it's annoying.

They are stylish and solid. Sub-$50 earbuds never feel this good, and they use their higher-quality materials in all the right places. Both the cable and the buds are light, but they're finished with a metallic material that is reassuringly sturdy. The design feels like it blends modern and retro aesthetics into something elegant.

They sound brilliant for the money. I liked their sound profile more than some buds that were far more expensive. Clean and smooth are the two words that come to mind: They're bassy enough for most people but it's in the mid-ranges and the splash of high notes that they come alive. They sound natural, no one element dominates, and their soundscape feels wide and detailed. I especially loved listening to the playful melodies of Astro Bot, punctuated by the ping of collecting coins.

They're surprisingly comfortable. I worried about the foam eartips, but I needn't. Their flat shape stayed fixed in my ear, never sliding around or rubbing against my skin. Some people are irritated by eartips sticking into their ear canal – this design avoids that problem.
